title: Independent Events and Unions of Events
rights: Original teacher-authored public-safe practice; no secure homework.

items.prompt: For one fair die, E is even and M is a multiple of 3. What is P(E and M)?
items.hint: Count numbers both even and multiples of 3.
items.solution: The intersection E∩M is {6}, so its probability is 1/6.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: With E and M from the previous question, what is P(E or M)?
items.hint: Use the union rule and subtract the overlap.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: Are E={2,4,6} and M={3,6} independent on a fair die?
items.hint: Compare the joint probability with the product of marginals.
items.solution: P(E∩M)=1/6=(3/6)(2/6), so E and M are independent, even though they overlap.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because all pairs of events from one die are independent.

items.prompt: Even and odd on a single fair-die roll are best described as which?
items.hint: Check whether they overlap and whether the independence product is zero.
items.solution: Even and odd are mutually exclusive since the intersection is zero, but are not independent since (3/6)(3/6)=1/4 is not zero.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: One card is selected from a standard deck. What is the probability it is a heart or a king?
items.hint: There is one king of hearts counted twice if you simply add.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: Suppose P(A)=0.45, P(B)=0.40, and P(A and B)=0.18. What is P(A or B)?
items.solution: P(A∪B)=0.45+0.40−0.18=0.67. These events are also independent because 0.45×0.40=0.18.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: Suppose P(A)=0.60, P(B)=0.50, and P(A and B)=0.20. Which statement is correct?
items.hint: Compare 0.20 with 0.60×0.50 and compute the union.
items.solution: P(A∪B)=0.60+0.50−0.20=0.90; P(A)P(B)=0.30, so the events are not independent.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

options.label: B
options.text: The events are independent and P(A or B)=0.80.

options.label: C
options.text: The events are dependent and P(A or B)=0.90.

items.prompt: A fair die is rolled three times independently. What is the probability of at least one six?
items.hint: Subtract P(no six on any of the three rolls) from 1.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026
